# R1. Sign-in and access

Everyone signs in; the signed-in person is who acts; the server enforces who may see and change what, with the rules Faro’s shared actions already enforce in code.

**Spec only.** Faro doesn’t build this: the internal app’s own platform provides the machinery, and this page says what it must do. It is part of the rebuild kit, not of Faro’s own requirements (`evals/requirements.json`).

## Why

Faro asks “Who are you?” once on each device and trusts the answer, and its public database key can still write to most tables (docs/mcp.md, “Until company sign-in arrives”). That is fine for a demo with made-up data and wrong for an app holding 15,000 people’s real goals: the change log must say who really did what, and a rule the browser checks can be skipped by anyone who calls the database directly.

The rules about who may do what already exist, once, in the shared actions the app and the AI assistant both call. The rebuild doesn’t need new rules; it needs them enforced where the records are stored, against a person the server knows.

## The rule

1. **Everyone signs in** (through the company’s sign-in, [R2](r2-single-sign-on.md)). There is no “Who are you?” and no “View as someone else”: the signed-in person is the actor for every action, and nobody chooses who they act as.
2. **Workspace membership is a person record.** A person belongs to a workspace when the workspace has a person record with their sign-in email (`Person.email`, lower case, one per workspace). Admins add people (Workspace or the People sheet); whoever creates a workspace is its first admin. Signing in with an email that matches no one: no workspace, and a message saying to ask an admin. Matching one: that workspace opens. Several: the person chooses. Marked as left (`leftAt`) or removed: no access to that workspace, and their MCP tokens stop working.
3. **Reading is open inside a workspace.** Every member reads every goal, check-in, plan, ask, review, comment, person, team and the Activity log of their workspace, as in Faro today: nothing in Faro hides a goal from a member. The exceptions, as Faro has them: the list of MCP tokens (an admin sees all, anyone else their own), Recently removed (an admin sees all, anyone else what they removed), the workspace’s feedback (admins), and the builder inbox (builders, rule 6; Faro opens its own on purpose). Someone who isn’t a member reads nothing of a workspace, not even that it exists.
4. **Changing follows the access table below**, which is what Faro’s shared actions enforce today. The server enforces it: a write the rules refuse is refused by the server (the database or the API), whatever sends it, with the same words the app shows. The browser’s own checks are only there to explain early. No key a browser holds can write.
5. **MCP tokens are made on the server.** An admin makes one for a person; the secret is made by the server, shown once, and only its SHA-256 hash is kept. A token belongs to one person in one workspace and acts with exactly that person’s rights (the same access table); every change it makes is logged as that person, marked via MCP. The token’s person or an admin revokes it; it stops working when its person leaves. A token can’t create, switch or reset a workspace or choose who it acts as.
6. **Builder tokens and the builder inbox.** Builders are the people who look after the app itself (in the internal app, a group in the company directory). Only builders read the builder inbox: the markups and feedback people send about the app, from every workspace. A builder makes a builder token for themselves; it reaches the inbox as well as their workspace, and stops counting as one the moment they leave the builders. Someone who sent a markup or feedback sees its status (New, In hand, Fixed, Won’t fix), not other people’s. **Faro differs on purpose:** it never holds real data, so its inbox is open to anyone (Lane, 8 Nov, backlog O); the internal app must not copy that. Faro keeps one Feedback inbox across workspaces, which anyone reads and only an admin triages: a status change from anyone else is refused by the rule (`statusPatch`, `mayTriage`; Lane, 12 Nov). **The rebuild scopes Feedback per workspace:** a workspace’s feedback is read and triaged by that workspace’s admins, and only the builder inbox crosses workspaces.
7. **Who may read a sent markup** (a markup about a goal sent to someone, backlog 3a). Its sender, the people it was sent to, and, when it was sent into a review, the people in that review. An admin of the workspace may remove one. Nobody else, watchers included. A markup is a picture of the sender’s screen, so it is only sent to people who can read everything on it: in the internal app, members of the same workspace. Its picture is kept private and read through a short-lived address the server makes for someone allowed to read it ([R4](r4-scale-and-safety.md), the master key).
8. **Exports are logged** (R-E1). An export (the workbook, the zipped CSVs, one sheet, JSON, the brief for an AI chat, a table from Data as shown, or the same through the AI assistant) follows the read rules of rule 3 and is written to the audit log with who, when and what: the file’s name, which goals (everything in the cycle, or a view and its filter) and which sheets. Exporting needs no right beyond reading, so nothing is refused; the log is so an admin can see what left the app and when.
9. **Opening the app without signing in shows the sign-in** (set-up spec SR1), never Welcome with a list of workspaces, a workspace or a name picker. After sign-in: no workspace, Welcome; one, its Home; several, the last one opened.
10. **An invitation is addressed to a person** (SR2). Adding someone to a workspace (their email, rule 2) is what invites them; the platform tells them by its own means (email, chat), with the same three lines Faro’s invitation has. Faro’s copy-and-paste link is the stand-in.
11. **Arriving is the first sign-in** (SR3). There is no “Which one are you?”: the signed-in email is matched to the person record. Someone with no record sees “You’re not in {workspace}. Ask {admins} to add you.” and nothing of the workspace. The server records the arrival at the first sign-in (the same log entry Faro writes when someone first chooses their name: `arrive`).
12. **The server checks every record kind, not every save.** A platform that stores rows (any database without Faro’s actions running beside it) must check each record a save writes against the stored rows before keeping it: who may write that kind (the access table), which fields are fixed once written, and which side-effect writes an action makes. The drill (item 11, 15 Nov) rebuilt Faro on a row store and found that a guard covering only goals, check-ins, people, teams, cycles, settings and views let a member forge decisions, retros, watches, asks, reviews and feedback, and that each module’s own guard still let side-effect writes through when the browser sent them along with a goal. The platform enforces this; the browser’s checks only explain early. The table **Record kinds the server checks** below lists every kind and every side-effect write as Faro’s actions make them today, and, apart, what a rebuild’s server should also check.

## Who may change what

Read from Faro’s shared actions: each line names the function that enforces it today, in the app and the AI assistant alike. `src/spec/internal.test.ts` fails when an action that says who may do something isn’t listed here. Anything not listed, any member may do.

### Record kinds the server checks

When a platform stores rows, with none of Faro’s actions running beside the store, each record a save writes is checked against the stored rows before it is kept (rule 12). The first three columns say what Faro’s actions do today (in the app and the MCP server; Faro’s own database checks much less): who may write the kind, which fields are fixed once written, and which side-effect writes an action makes, which the server makes itself, never taking them from the browser. A server that allows less refuses saves Faro makes. The last column, **A rebuild should also check**, is what the drill (item 11) found a rebuild’s server should add beyond Faro; it is kept apart, never part of what Faro does.

| Record kind | Who may write it (Faro today) | Fixed once written (Faro today) | Side-effect writes the server makes itself (Faro today) | A rebuild should also check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| People (`people`) | Admins add someone and change their name, job title, team, email or admin rights (the only admin stays one). A person writes their own record only by leaving; arriving writes a change-log entry and no record. Marking someone as left, or deleting someone with no history: admins, never themselves or the only admin. Restoring: an admin, or whoever removed them | id, workspace; an email can be changed, never taken away, and no two people share one | Someone leaving (marked as left, or leaving themselves) hands their goals in this cycle and any later one to whoever takes over, hands the open asks they raised or must answer to whoever takes those, takes them out of the reviews they were in, and passes the teams they led to whoever takes their goals. Their watches are kept. Deleting someone with no history takes them out of reviews and team leads. Undoing an import puts back or removes the people it changed or added. | Who is acting comes from the sign-in, never from the save (SR3). |
| Goals (`goals`) | Adding: anyone, for anyone, at any level. Changing (name, plan, owner, unit, decimals): its owner, an admin, or while it is proposed whoever proposed it. Stopping or deleting: its owner or an admin (a proposal also whoever proposed it). Making a proposed goal active: its owner or an admin. Proposing one in a review: someone in it, or an admin. Restoring: an admin, or whoever removed it | id, key, cycle, when it was created | Starting the next year writes the copies of the goals that carry on. A check-in, wrap-up or change on a goal of a year that has a later one rewrites, takes out or brings back its copy there while nobody has used the copy, whoever owns it. Stopping or deleting a goal moves the goals feeding it up to what it fed and takes it off other goals’ “also helps”. Someone leaving hands their goals over. Removing a team moves its goals (removed ones too) to another team. A goal that changes owner hands its open asks for an update and questions to the new owner, or withdraws the ones the new owner asked, in the goal’s own save. A new goal saved by its owner with stages already done writes a set-up check-in in the same save. Undoing an import writes back the goals, people, asks, reviews and teams it changed, and its module rows. The metric library: a relabel changes the unit of the goals a metric measures; a gap opened or closed (a metric saved, retired, brought back or merged, or a goal linked or unlinked) holds goals to no number or to their plans again, whoever owns them; switching the library off lets go of every goal it held, and on holds them again. | Record who created a goal and keep it fixed (Faro keeps no creator). Accept a goal proposed in a review only as that review’s change, never riding another save. |
| Check-ins (`checkIns`) | The goal’s owner, at every door. Two exceptions, both an admin’s: a workbook (an import, or setting up from an export) brings in past weeks or corrects one there, and Data’s tables correct one that exists. Deleting: the goal’s owner, and only its latest. Undoing an import: whoever made it, or an admin, as the access table says. Restoring: an admin, or whoever removed it | goal, week, who posted it (a correction keeps them; History names who corrected it, and why) | In the same save as the check-in: its goal’s open asks for an update are answered; with a decision or help in it, the goal’s open one carries on (its words changed if they differ) or a new one is raised, and the goal’s own open one to someone else is withdrawn; without one, the goal’s own open decision or help is withdrawn and its link to another goal’s is dropped. On a goal of a year that has a later one, its untouched copy follows (as for Goals). Deleting a check-in withdraws an open ask it raised. A new goal saved by its owner with stages already done writes a set-up check-in in the goal’s save. Undoing an import puts back or deletes the check-ins it wrote. | Set when a check-in was posted from the server’s clock. |
| Decisions (what is said in a review) (`decisions`) | Seen, a note, accepting the risk and marking goals reviewed: someone in the review, or an admin, about a goal it walks, as themselves. Correcting or removing a note: whoever said it, or an admin. Undoing goals marked reviewed: whoever marked them, or an admin. Restoring a note: an admin, or whoever removed it | who said it, when, its goal, its review and week | None. | Set when it was said from the server’s clock. |
| Asks (`requests`) | A decision or help: raised, changed and withdrawn by its goal’s check-in, so by whoever may check in on the goal (its owner, or an admin by a workbook or Data’s tables). | Cycles (`cycles`) | Admins: start the next year (from the day the wrap-up opens; once), undo the start while nobody has used it, delete a year no one has checked in to, choose the check-in rhythm. Restoring: an admin, or whoever removed it | id, workspace | Starting the next year writes the copies of the goals that carry on, and with them a watch for each watch of a carried goal or tree, each carried goal’s copy added to its open asks and to the reviews that walk it, and the module rows that follow a goal (a metric link). Undoing the start removes the year’s goals’ watches and module rows, and puts the asks and reviews back as they were. Deleting a year writes only the year: its goals go and come back with it. | None beyond these. |
| Watches (`watches, unwatch`) | Watching and stopping: each person their own only; nobody, admins included, starts or stops someone else’s. A copy that leaves a later year stops its watches, and one that comes back is watched again. While Watching is off, a save that writes a watch is refused, except those carried along this way. | Make the carried watches on the server, and refuse a watch for someone else sent with a goal. |
| Saved views (`views`) | Anyone saves their own; its owner or an admin changes or deletes it; admins pin; restoring: an admin, or whoever deleted it | its owner, workspace, when it was made, and whether it is a view of Goals or of a data table | None. | None beyond these. |
| Tokens (`tokens`) | Made by an admin for anyone in the workspace. The app’s action refuses while AI access is off; the database function (okr_token_create) checks only that the token’s maker is an admin, not the switch (a backlog bug). Revoked by its person or an admin, also while AI access is off. Changed otherwise only by use, which moves its last use | its person, workspace, hash, who made it, when | None. | Refuse making a token while AI access is off, in the database too. Builder tokens (rule 6). |
| Feedback and markups (`feedback`) | Anyone adds, as themselves; the database drops any status a save sends, so it arrives New. A status is changed only by an admin (`mayTriage`), any admin, over the one inbox every workspace shares; the check is in Faro’s code (the app and the MCP server), not the database’s | sender, workspace, text, when | None. | Scope Feedback per workspace: only that workspace’s admins triage its feedback, checked on the server, and only builders read the builder inbox (rule 6). |
| Teams, the workspace’s name, recording and feature switches (`teams, removeTeams, workspace, recording, modulesOff`) | Admins of that workspace | id, workspace | Removing a team moves its people and goals to the team chosen (removed goals to it, or else to the first other team). Someone leaving passes the teams they led to whoever takes their goals; deleting someone clears their lead. Switching a feature off or on saves, in the same save, what each module switched needs of the core’s records: today only the metric library, which lets go of every goal it held to no number when off and holds them again when on. Every module’s own rows are kept. Undoing an import puts back the teams it changed and removes the ones it added once nothing sits in them. | None beyond these. |
| The change log (`changes`) | Written by each action as the person acting, in the same save as what it describes. Some entries stand alone, with no record beside them: a comment, its edit, removal and restore, and someone arriving | everything: an entry is never changed | None. | Take the person acting from the sign-in, never from the save, and keep an entry only beside the change it describes, or as one of the entries that stand alone. |
| Module rows (`modules`) | Each module’s own actions (the metric library’s metrics and goal links; Fields’ fields and their values), refused by the app’s actions and the MCP server’s tools while the module is switched off; a build without the module has none. The database refuses a table no module declares, and doesn’t check the switch (a backlog bug) | as each module says | As each module says: a metric link follows a carried goal into the next year and leaves with its copy; undoing the start removes it. Undoing an import puts back the module rows it wrote. | Refuse a module’s rows on the server while it is switched off or left out of the build, whatever marks the save carries; refuse an unknown kind or key, not ignore it. Import jobs’ rows by job. |
| Files (`files`) | Only a markup’s pictures: uploaded into a folder named like a markup id, only its four pictures, png or jpeg up to 5 MB, never replaced or deleted. Anyone may read them (a public bucket) | the path, once written | None. | Scope files to a workspace and to whoever may read them; an import’s upload only to its job; readings drops only by admins; normalise the path before any check. |

The values the database checks today are part of the check: the allowed moods and statuses, lengths, and dates set by the server’s clock. They are in [`spec/core/schema.sql`](../../core/schema.sql); timestamps written by the server are [R3](r3-time-zones.md).

## What Faro does today

- The app asks “Who are you?” and remembers the answer on the device (Help, “Saying who you are”; `src/screens/Start.tsx`).
- Every rule in the access table is checked in `src/domain/actions.ts`, `src/domain/removal.ts`, `src/domain/asks.ts` and the change engine (`src/domain/changeset.ts`), by the app and the MCP server alike, before anything is saved. The database doesn’t check them.
- The public key can still write to most tables (not tokens; it can only add markups and feedback). Tokens are made in the database by `okr_token_create` and found by hash (`okr_token_find`, migration 0024).
- Every grant, row rule and `security definer` function the database has today is listed in one place, read from the database after every migration and each marked “demo access: replace”: [access today](../../rebuild/access-today.md). It ends with the two shapes that replace them: a membership rule on each table, and a definer function that checks who is calling before it does anything.
- A browser that remembers no workspace opens Welcome at its own address, `/welcome`, never a workspace nobody chose; an invitation is a link, `/join/<workspace>`, that opens the arrival screen: who set the workspace up, then “Which one are you?”, where anyone may choose any name, the admin’s included (`src/screens/Welcome.tsx`, `src/screens/Start.tsx`, `invitedTo` and `inviteLink` in `src/domain/dayOne.ts`, the arrival’s lines in `src/domain/arrival.ts`). Choosing a name the first time writes the arrival to the log (`arrive` in `src/domain/actions.ts`).
- Every workspace in the shared database is listed to anyone who opens the app (`SupabaseStore.workspaces` in `src/adapters/supabase/goalsStore.ts`).
- Faro’s inbox is open on purpose (backlog O, migration 0031): anyone, with no sign-in, reads every markup and piece of feedback and their pictures (a public-read bucket nobody can list), and changes a status through the one status rule, recorded as the person using the app and undoable; any token reaches it through MCP. There is no builder sign-in and no builder token in the app any more (the builders list and builder tokens from migrations 0024 and 0029 are left in the database, unused). The internal app keeps rule 6 as written.
- Markups today are reports about the app; sending one about a goal (3a) is not built yet.
- Export is open to everyone in a workspace and isn’t logged: the file is made in the browser (`src/modules/spreadsheets/Export.tsx`, `src/domain/export.ts`) and the MCP server’s `export` and `export_table` (`src/modules/spreadsheets/tools.ts`), and nothing is written to the change log (import spec 2.9, decision 7).

## Worked examples

An example marked **Faro today** is run against Faro’s code by `src/spec/internal.test.ts`: the result is what the code gives now. The others say what the internal app must do.

| Given | Then | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| Maya, not an admin, makes an MCP token for herself. | refused: “Only admins can make tokens.” | **Faro today** |
| Maya, not an admin, changes Oskar’s job title. | refused: “Only admins can add people or change them.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar, not an admin, renames the workspace. | refused: “Only admins can rename the workspace.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar, not an admin, deletes the workspace, giving its name exactly. | refused: “Only admins can delete the workspace.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar asked Maya for a decision. May Oskar, Maya and Priya (an admin) answer it? | Oskar no, Maya yes, Priya yes | **Faro today** |
| Priya asked Oskar to do an action. May Oskar, Priya and Maya mark it done? | Oskar yes, Priya yes, Maya no | **Faro today** |
| Oskar raised a decision on Maya’s goal, and also asked her for an update on it. May Maya withdraw each? | the decision yes, the update no | **Faro today** |
| Oskar opens Platform for the first time from the invitation and chooses his name. | the log says “Oskar Lind opened Platform for the first time”; choosing again adds nothing | **Faro today** |
| Someone opens the internal app with no sign-in, holding Platform’s invitation. | The sign-in, then Platform’s Home as the person with their email; no Welcome, no list of workspaces and no “Which one are you?”. | Required |
| Someone signs in whose email is on no person in Platform, holding Platform’s invitation. | “You’re not in Platform. Ask Priya Shah to add you.” and nothing of the workspace. | Required |
| Someone signs in as Maya.Patel@Example.com, and Maya’s person record has maya.patel@example.com. | They are Maya: emails are compared in lower case. | Required |
| Oskar is marked as left in Platform, and still has a token. | He can’t open Platform, and his token is refused at once. | Required |
| Maya sends a markup of her goal’s chart to Oskar. | Maya and Oskar can read it; Priya, an admin, can remove it but it isn’t in her list; someone watching the goal can’t see it. | Required |
| A script with the browser’s public key writes a check-in to Maya’s goal. | The server refuses it: the public key can’t write. | Required |
| Oskar, not an admin, exports everything in the cycle as a workbook. | It downloads, and the audit log gains one entry: Oskar, the time, the file’s name, “everything in Year 2026”, and its sheets. Priya, an admin, sees it. | Required |

## Acceptance checks

1. For every line of the access table, someone outside its “who” is refused by the server, called directly with their own sign-in (not through the app), with the words the app shows. Someone inside it is allowed.
2. Every table refuses a write made with the public key, and every read of a workspace by someone who isn’t a member returns nothing.
3. Opening the app without signing in shows the sign-in, never a workspace or a list of workspaces.
4. A person an admin marks as left in the app can’t open the workspace, and a request with their token is refused within a minute of being marked. (Leaving the company through the directory is R2’s, check 4: within the company’s policy, an hour at most.)
5. A token’s secret appears once, in the answer that made it, and nowhere stored: the database holds its SHA-256 hash.
6. Every change in the change log names the signed-in person (or the token’s person, marked via MCP); no change names someone else.
7. In the internal app: a builder token reads the builder inbox; an ordinary token, an admin’s included, is told it isn’t a builder token. Removing a builder from the builders stops their token reaching the inbox at once. (Faro’s open inbox fails this check on purpose.)
8. A sent markup is readable by its sender, its recipients and (sent into a review) the review’s people, and by nobody else; its picture’s address stops working after it expires.
9. Every export, from the app or through the AI assistant, writes one audit entry with who, when, the file’s name, which goals and which sheets; an export by someone outside the workspace returns nothing and writes nothing.

## Nearest rebuild stage

[Stage 2: the core data and the change engine](../../rebuild/stage-2-core-data.md): access is enforced where the records are stored and changed. The rules themselves are the shared actions and the change engine; stage 3’s screens only explain them.

## Decided while writing it

- Reading stays open to every member of a workspace, as in Faro; private goals would be a new product rule, not in Faro.
- A sent markup is read by its sender, recipients and (in a review) the review’s people; not by watchers. Admins can remove one. This answers 3a’s open question on watchers for the internal app.
- Only admins make MCP tokens, as Faro’s code says today; anyone revokes their own.
- Faro opens its inbox to anyone (Lane, 8 Nov): it holds no real data, and Lane needs to read markups on any device. The internal app keeps the inbox to builders (rule 6).
